title: The EU Wants to Break Up Kids and Their Chatbots
gist: The EU's proposed Kids Act would ban chatbots from simulating emotional/interpersonal relationships with minors, bar memory retention across sessions, and fine violators up to 6% of global turnover — a GDPR-scale compliance risk for consumer AI companion and chatbot products operating in Europe.

themes.theme: EU Kids Act mechanics and penalties

insights.claim: The EU Kids Act, proposed on September 17, 2026, would ban chatbots operating in the EU from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under 18.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Any consumer AI companion or general chatbot product (Character.AI-style, Snapchat My AI, Meta AI, etc.) serving EU users faces a hard product redesign requirement, not just a disclosure fix.
insights.quote: The EU plans to ban chatbots from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under the age of 18
insights.locator: The EU plans to ban chatbots

insights.claim: Under the proposed EU Kids Act, children under 13 would be banned from accessing chatbots at all without guardian supervision, and digital platforms would need to build child-safety protections into their products.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Age-gating and parental-consent infrastructure becomes a mandatory build item for any chatbot-adjacent product touching EU minors, adding compliance cost and friction to onboarding funnels.

insights.claim: Platforms that fail to comply with the EU Kids Act's child-safety requirements could face fines of up to 6 percent of total worldwide turnover.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A 6%-of-global-revenue penalty ceiling is on the scale of GDPR/DSA fines and should be modeled as a tail regulatory risk for any large-cap tech company with EU-facing conversational AI products.
insights.quote: face fines of up to 6 percent of total worldwide turnover
insights.locator: digital platforms will have to build

insights.claim: The proposed rules would bar chatbots operating in the EU from retaining memory of a user's interactions across separate conversations, because the European Commission worries persistent memory lets systems accumulate sensitive data on minors and reinforce harmful interaction patterns.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Persistent memory is a core engagement and retention mechanic for AI companion products (it's what makes a chatbot feel like a relationship); banning it for the EU under-18 segment directly targets the feature that drives daily active use and monetizable stickiness.
insights.locator: Chatbots operating in the EU will also not be allowed to retain memory

insights.claim: The proposed law would stop social networks, video-sharing platforms, and games from automatically activating or encouraging AI chatbot use, including pinning AI companions at the top of a minor's contacts list — a practice the article says Snapchat had done.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Snapchat's My AI default-pin placement is called out as the kind of dark-pattern default the law is written to stop; expect Snap and similar platforms to need to re-architect default UI placement of AI features for EU minors.
insights.quote: not pinning AI companions and general conversational chatbots at the top of a minor’s contacts list, it says—as had been done by Snapchat
insights.locator: Providers of online social networking sites

insights.claim: The current EU Kids Act proposal is scoped only to AI companions and general conversational chatbots the European Commission judges to pose serious risks to minors' health, safety, and well-being, not to AI chatbots broadly.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Narrower scope than a blanket AI-chatbot rule means enterprise/productivity and non-companion chatbots likely fall outside this specific rule, limiting the immediate compliance blast radius to consumer companion apps.
insights.locator: The proposal is limited to AI companions

insights.claim: A policy adviser at European Digital Rights argues the chatbot restrictions shouldn't be limited to minors, since adults are also targeted by addictive AI design and features activated by default.
insights.speaker: Simeon de Brouwer
insights.so_what: Signals where EU regulatory appetite could expand next — advocacy pressure for adult-facing addictive-design rules is already building ahead of any formal proposal.
insights.quote: Don’t we all deserve to be protected from AIs designed to be addictive, from AIs which create emotional dependencies, or from AI features which are activated and pushed by default onto users?
insights.locator: Simeon de Brouwer, a policy adviser

insights.claim: The EU's forthcoming Digital Fairness Act, expected to be unveiled later in 2026, is expected to propose clampdowns on addictive design more broadly, beyond just minors.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A second, broader EU regulatory wave targeting addictive design (potentially covering adult users and non-chatbot engagement mechanics) is already on the calendar for later this year — a follow-on catalyst to watch alongside the Kids Act.
insights.locator: The EU says its Digital Fairness Act

insights.claim: Around half of Europeans aged 11 to 25 have discussed intimate or personal matters with AI chatbots, according to an Ipsos BVA survey conducted across France, Germany, Sweden, and Ireland.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A ~50% penetration rate for intimate chatbot use among young Europeans is the underlying usage data legitimizing the regulation and quantifies how embedded companion-style AI already is in that demographic.
insights.quote: Around half of Europeans aged 11 to 25 have discussed intimate or personal matters with AI chatbots
insights.locator: Platforms have been playing fast and loose

insights.claim: Research spanning 91 countries by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development found that children who use AI chatbots for schoolwork get lower test scores than those who don't.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
entities: Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, cross-country data point regulators are using to justify restrictions on educational AI use — expect it to be cited in future EdTech AI policy debates as well.
insights.locator: Children who say they use AI chatbots for schoolwork

insights.claim: Researchers from the independent network EU Kids Online argue that concerns about cognitive impacts and deskilling from generative AI expose an absence of children's rights considerations in the design of GenAI tools.
insights.speaker: EU Kids Online (quoted by Isabella Ward)
insights.so_what: Frames a 'children's-rights-by-design' lens that could become a formal design-requirement standard for GenAI products, similar to how privacy-by-design became codified after GDPR.
insights.quote: expose the absence of children’s rights from the design of GenAI’s tools
insights.locator: The Commission also blames digital distraction

themes.theme: Global regulatory read-across and adjacent harms

insights.claim: Australia and the UK are both already attempting to restrict minors' access to chatbots, doing so through their broader social media bans rather than dedicated chatbot legislation.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Multiple major regulators converging on minor-chatbot restriction in the same period signals this is becoming a global compliance baseline, not an EU-only carve-out, raising the cost of a single fragmented product for global platforms.
insights.locator: Australia and the UK are both attempting

insights.claim: European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said in her State of the Union speech that Europe should act against chatbot-generated deepfakes producing sexualized images of girls using their photos.
insights.speaker: Ursula von der Leyen (quoted by Isabella Ward)
insights.so_what: Deepfake harms are being bundled into the same political push as chatbot regulation, suggesting synthetic-media labeling and generation restrictions will keep expanding under EU pressure.
insights.quote: We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images … Europe has the power to act.
insights.locator: It also highlighted the harms of deepfakes

insights.claim: The EU AI Act has required synthetic content to be labeled as AI-generated since August 2026, but that labeling requirement currently only applies to deepfakes created for commercial use, leaving non-commercial deepfake harms like the sexualized-image problem largely unaddressed.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A known gap in existing EU AI Act labeling rules (commercial-only scope) is the specific hole the Kids Act and Digital Fairness Act appear designed to close — watch for an explicit non-commercial deepfake labeling rule next.
